web_title: 6. 6-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Behind the 40% Margin — Lease Leverage, Dilution & Cash Forensics
question: What do six years of P&L, balance-sheet, cash-flow, and shareholding forensics reveal about Afcom's financial durability and promoter alignment?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion; operating cash flow after lease payments and receivables is the only truth an airline balance sheet cannot hide.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: From FY21 to H1 FY27, Afcom Holdings posted one of the fastest sales ramps in Indian air cargo [1, 17]. Revenue grew from ₹13.89 crore in FY21 to ₹241.01 crore in FY25 and ₹583.00 crore in FY26 [1, 17]. H1 FY27 sales reached ₹417.00 crore [1, 20]. Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) rose from 21% in FY25 to 28% in FY26 [1, 16]. Yet the balance sheet and cash-flow statement show three key weak spots [1, 9, 10]. Those risks are **Ind AS 116 lease debt**, **weak CFO-to-PAT conversion**, and **repeated share dilution** [1, 9, 10].

web_blocks.caption: Afcom Holdings: 6-Year Financial Forensics & Cash Conversion (FY21–FY26 + H1 FY27, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue grew 42x from FY21 to FY26 and PAT hit ₹122 Cr, yet cumulative FY25–FY26 CFO was -₹9 Cr against -₹464 Cr of investing outflows, requiring continuous external equity and lease financing.

web_blocks.html: First, under Ind AS 116, Afcom's 96-month dry leases add ~₹306 crore of Right-of-Use (ROU) assets and **₹338 crore of lease debt** [10, 20]. Total assets topped ₹935 crore in FY26 and ₹1,204 crore by September 2026 [10, 20]. Standalone borrowings (~₹40.07 crore in FY26) look small next to ₹234 crore of EBITDA [9, 10]. Including leases, leverage is ~1.6x, backing an Acuité BBB+ stable rating, yet lease bills remain fixed dollar-linked claims [9, 10]. Second, CFO lagged PAT badly: -₹45 crore CFO vs. ₹36.94 crore PAT in FY25, and just 29.5% in FY26 (₹36 crore CFO vs. ₹122 crore PAT) [9, 16]. Rising ~85-day receivables and working capital absorbed that cash [9, 16].

web_blocks.caption: Afcom Holdings: Shareholding Shift & Institutionalization (Sep 2024 – Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Promoter stake fell 733 bps (42.73% to 35.40%) primarily due to May 2026 QIP and preferential dilution rather than founder exits, while DII ownership jumped from 0.85% to 7.61%.

web_blocks.html: Third, the shareholding table shows steady equity dilution [1]. Promoter stake held at 42.73% through June 2025, then slipped to 40.61% in March 2026 and 35.40% by September 2026 [1]. Exchange filings show this 7.33-point drop came mostly from **new share sales**, not founder selling [10, 12, 19]. Key deals were the May 2026 QIP (26.31 lakh shares, ₹199.84 crore), a preferential issue (12.10 lakh shares, ₹104.47 crore), and warrant conversions [10, 12]. Capt. Deepak Parasuraman kept his core stake [19]. Meanwhile, DII ownership jumped from 0.85% in March 2026 to 7.96% in June 2026 and 7.61% in September 2026 [1]. Bandhan Mutual Fund (~22.52% of the QIP), Abakkus Emerging Opportunities Fund, and Ashish Kacholia led that buying [1, 12]. Fresh equity eased near-term cash risk, yet future per-share gains require CFO to fund fleet growth internally.

Lease accounting under Ind AS 116 also shapes FY26 cash flows [13, 14]. ROU assets sit at ₹306.00 crore against ₹338.00 crore of lease debt [13, 14]. Lease principal payments go under Financing Cash Flow, not Operating Cash Flow [14]. Meanwhile, lease interest (₹32.00 crore in FY26) and depreciation (₹53.00 crore) hit the P&L [10, 14]. Even before lease principal payments, FY26 CFO was just ₹36.00 crore against ₹122.00 crore PAT [9, 14]. Receivable growth and security deposits consumed the rest [9, 14].

The gap between 28% ROCE in FY26 (up from 21% in FY25) and -₹170.71 crore Free Cash Flow defines Afcom's balance-sheet puzzle [1, 14, 15]. Accounting returns look strong when planes fly full [1]. Still, until working capital settles and growth capex slows, free cash flow—not ROCE—limits self-funded growth [9, 16]. That is why Q3 and full-year FY27 cash conversion is the key test. Seeing CFO/PAT top 40% (and ideally 50%) would prove QIP cash stabilized operations rather than masking ongoing burn. Clean cash generation would also remove the need for another round of equity dilution [10, 12]. Only then can strong accounting returns turn into lasting per-share wealth.

book_paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic-accounting hat and look behind Afcom's headline numbers. Between FY21 and FY26, revenue multiplied more than fortyfold, from ₹13.89 crore to ₹583 crore, and return on capital employed reached 28%. Those are eye-catching figures. Yet when you and I open the cash-flow statement and the balance sheet, three critical realities emerge.

First, Afcom's aircraft are not free—they sit on the balance sheet under Ind AS 116 as roughly ₹306 crore of Right-of-Use assets paired with ₹338 crore of lease liabilities. Those are multi-year, dollar-linked commitments that must be paid whether cargo demand is booming or soft. Second, cash conversion has lagged accounting profit by a wide margin. In FY25, Afcom reported ₹36.94 crore of net profit but burned ₹45 crore in operating cash flow. In FY26, it reported ₹122 crore of net profit but generated just ₹36 crore of operating cash flow—less than thirty paise on the rupee—because 85-day customer receivables and fleet deposits soaked up cash.

book_callouts.title: DILUTION WATCH: PROMOTER STAKE AT 35.40%
book_callouts.text: Promoter ownership dropped from 42.73% at IPO to 35.40% by September 2026. While driven largely by growth-equity QIP and preferential raises that brought in Bandhan Mutual Fund and marquee DIIs, any further equity dilution below 30% would weaken founder alignment.

book_subsections.title: Decoding the Promoter Stake Decline and DII Entry
paragraphs: At first glance, seeing promoter ownership drop from 42.73% in September 2024 to 35.40% in September 2026 raises an immediate red flag. Did the founders cash out? The filings show a more nuanced picture. The bulk of the drop occurred in the June 2026 quarter, coinciding directly with the May 2026 QIP of ₹199.84 crore, a ₹104.47 crore preferential share allotment, and subsequent warrant conversions. Rather than dumping shares into retail hands, Captain Deepak Parasuraman remained anchored while domestic institutional investors—led by Bandhan Mutual Fund, Abakkus, and Ashish Kacholia—pushed DII ownership from under 1% to nearly 8%.

Even so, serial equity dilution is a double-edged sword. Equity raises kept debt manageable while funding ₹464 crore of cumulative investing outflows across FY25 and FY26, and total assets crossed ₹1,204 crore by September 2026. Going forward, the single biggest forensic test for Afcom is whether operating cash flow converges toward net profit so that the fourth and fifth narrowbodies—and any future widebodies—are funded by internal cash rather than another round of share issuance.

book_subsections.title: The Price-Blind Business Quality Verdict
paragraphs: Before we ever look at a stock chart or a valuation multiple, we owe ourselves an honest verdict on business quality. Afcom is not a fragile shell company—it has built real operational credibility, a profitable India–ASEAN niche, and institutional backing. At the same time, 30% cash conversion, 85-day receivables, heavy lease liabilities, and reliance on cyclical charter demand mean this is not an effortless asset-light compounder. It earns a conditional cyclical pass: strong execution, with cash conversion and fleet discipline firmly on watch.

book_subsections.title: How Ind AS 116 Lease Accounting Masks Cash Burn
paragraphs: Let us linger on one accounting detail that trips up almost every generalist investor looking at an airline: Ind AS 116 lease accounting. On Afcom's FY26 balance sheet, Right-of-Use assets sit at ₹306 crore against ₹338 crore of lease liabilities. Under accounting rules, lease depreciation of ₹53 crore and lease interest of ₹32 crore flow through the income statement, while the actual principal portion of monthly aircraft lease payments is tucked away inside Financing Cash Flows.

That means Reported Operating Cash Flow actually flatters a dry-leased airline compared to a company that pays rent straight through operating expenses. Yet even with that accounting tailwind, Afcom's FY26 operating cash flow was just ₹36 crore against ₹122 crore of reported net profit—a 29.5 percent conversion ratio—while investing cash outflows hit -₹206.71 crore. Until receivables shrink from 85 days and security deposits stop absorbing every rupee of profit, Afcom's financial engine remains dependent on external capital.

book_subsections.title: Reconciling 28 Percent ROCE With Negative Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: On paper, a 28 percent Return on Capital Employed in FY26—up from 21 percent in FY25—looks like the hallmark of a capital-efficient compounder. Yet in that same fiscal year, Afcom generated -₹170.71 crore of free cash flow once ₹206.71 crore of investing outflows were netted against ₹36 crore of operating cash flow.

How can both numbers be true at once? Because ROCE measures operating profit against deployed capital on the balance sheet, whereas free cash flow captures the upfront cash consumed by aircraft lease deposits, entry-into-service capex, and 85-day customer receivables while the fleet is tripling in size. That gap is precisely why our price-blind verdict is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL rather than an unconditional pass.

With Chapters 1 through 6 complete, our price-blind foundation is locked. Afcom is a genuine operational breakout on the income statement—scaling revenue fortyfold from FY21 to FY26—yet its 29.5 percent CFO-to-PAT conversion, 85-day receivables, ₹338 crore lease liabilities, and serial equity dilution place it squarely in the CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL tier.

Keep that six-year financial table in mind whenever you hear an analyst cite Afcom's 40 percent EBITDA margin. Margin without cash conversion is only half the story, and Q3 FY27 will show whether working-capital friction is finally easing.
